issue_title: Multi-agent systems need a 'mission keeper' role — not a Boss Agent, but a dedicated goal integrity node
issue_body: There's a classic CS joke: `git blame` tells you who wrote the code, but it can't tell you *why it made sense at the time*. Multi-agent systems have the same problem — by the time a task finishes, nobody can tell you whether the final output still matches the original intent. The intermediate agents each did their job. The goal just quietly drifted somewhere along the way. --- **The structural gap I keep hitting with the current SelectorGroupChat design:** AutoGen's Planning Agent is doing two things at once: - Coordinating execution (assigning tasks, sequencing agents) - Keeping track of whether the original goal is still being honored These two responsibilities have very different failure modes. Coordination failure is loud — tasks get dropped, agents deadlock, TERMINATE never fires. Goal drift is silent — every agent reports success, the workflow completes cleanly, and the output is coherent but wrong in a way that only becomes apparent later. Mixing both into one Planning Agent means that when coordination gets complex (which it always does), goal integrity gets deprioritized. It's just cognitive load — the planner is managing traffic while also trying to remember where everyone was supposed to be going. --- **The analogy that makes this concrete:** Distributed systems solved a version of this in the 80s. Paxos and Raft aren't about making nodes smarter — they're about designating *which node's version of truth wins* when nodes disagree. issue_title: Cryptographic governance layer for AutoGen distributed agent runtime
issue_body: AutoGen's distributed agent runtime enables powerful multi-agent systems, but currently lacks cryptographic identity and authority enforcement between agents. **Problem**: When Agent A sends a message to Agent B in a distributed runtime, there's no cryptographic proof of: - Who Agent A actually is (identity) - What Agent A is authorized to request (delegation scope) - Whether Agent A's authority is still valid (revocation status) - What happened after Agent B acted (audit receipt) **Proposal**: Integrate the Agent Passport System as a governance layer for the distributed runtime: 1. Each agent gets an Ed25519 passport (identity) 2. Inter-agent messages carry signed delegation chains (authority) 3. ProxyGateway validates identity + scope before message delivery (enforcement) 4. Every action generates a signed ActionReceipt (audit) 5. Reputation-Gated Authority caps effective permissions based on earned trust The Agent Passport System ships 16 protocol modules, 534 tests, and 61 MCP tools. Apache 2.0. GitHub: https://github.com/aeoess/agent-passport-system Spec: https://aeoess.com/llms-full.txt Paper: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18749779 Happy to discuss integration architecture. cc @imran-siddique who is already exploring governance patterns for Microsoft agent frameworks.

issue_body: ### Problem When a tool call takes longer than ~3 minutes on LangGraph Cloud, it gets silently re-dispatched from the last checkpoint while the original is still running. Both the original and the duplicate complete successfully, resulting in 2-3x redundant work and cost. We're using deepagents' `SubAgentMiddleware`, where the main agent dispatches sub-agents via a `task()` tool that internally calls `subagent.ainvoke()`. issue_title: [Feature Request]: Memory poisoning defense (OWASP ASI06) integration for agent memory stores
issue_body: ### Feature Description OWASP recently published the **Top 10 for Agentic Applications**, which includes **ASI06: Memory Poisoning** — a threat specific to AI agents that persist memory across sessions. LlamaIndex's agent memory stores (ChatMemoryBuffer, VectorMemory, SimpleComposableMemory) are a prime target for this attack. A malicious user can craft inputs that get stored as "trusted" memories, which then influence future agent behavior — leaking data, taking unauthorized actions, or hijacking tool calls across sessions. The OWASP reference implementation for ASI06 is [agent-memory-guard](https://github.com/OWASP/www-project-agent-memory-guard) (Apache-2.0, pure Python, zero external dependencies): pip install agent-memory-guard Proposed integration: A GuardedMemory wrapper that implements LlamaIndex's BaseMemory interface, screening all put() and get() calls through the OWASP defense pipeline (prompt injection detection, integrity verification, policy enforcement). ### Reason LlamaIndex currently has no built-in defense for memory poisoning attacks. As agent use cases grow (especially multi-session, multi-user deployments), this becomes a critical security gap. The OWASP ASI06 reference implementation provides a drop-in solution. ### Value of Feature Provides OWASP-compliant memory security for LlamaIndex agents. Addresses a formally recognized threat category (ASI06) with a production-ready, zero-dependency implementation. Enables enterprise adoption of LlamaIndex agents where security compliance is required.

issue_title: Feature: Cryptographic action receipts (AAR) for provable agent execution
issue_body: ## Problem When LangGraph agents execute multi-step workflows, there's no standardized way to cryptographically prove what happened at each node. Audit logs exist, but they're mutable and unsigned — a compromised system can rewrite history without detection. For regulated domains (finance, healthcare, legal), this is a blocker. Compliance teams need tamper-proof evidence that Agent X performed Action Y with Input Z at Time T. ## Proposal: Agent Action Receipt (AAR) Integration AAR is a lightweight spec for Ed25519-signed receipts that capture agent actions with cryptographic integrity: ```json { "receiptId": "uuid", "agent": "langgraph-node-analyzer", "action": "analyze_document", "inputHash": "sha256-of-input", "outputHash": "sha256-of-output", "timestamp": "2026-03-08T15:00:00Z", "signature": "ed25519-detached-signature" } ``` Key properties: - **Offline verifiable** — deterministic canonical JSON, single `nacl.sign.detached.verify()` call - **PII-free** — SHA-256 hashes of inputs/outputs, never raw data - **Composable** — receipts chain via Session Continuity Certificates (SCC) for cross-session provenance ## Integration surface for LangGraph Each graph node execution could emit an AAR receipt. The natural hook is the `RunnableConfig` callbacks — a `AARCallbackHandler` that signs receipts at node boundaries. ## Resources - Spec: https://github.com/Cyberweasel777/agent-action-receipt-spec - SDK: https://www.npmjs.com/package/botindex-aar (115+ daily downloads) - Hosted signing: https://botindex.dev (for teams that don't want to manage keys) - Active discussion: crewAI #47

The failure is logged at `WARNING` level but **no exception is raised to the caller**, so the application has no way to know that a fact extracted by the LLM was never persisted. issue_title: [Security] Web Surfer agent vulnerable to indirect prompt injection via page title
issue_body: ## [Security] Web Surfer agent vulnerable to indirect prompt injection via page title ### Summary The `MultimodalWebSurfer` agent embeds attacker-controlled webpage metadata (`<title>` tag and URL) directly into LLM prompts without sanitization, enabling indirect prompt injection from any visited website. **Severity**: MEDIUM **Rule**: AGENT-010 — Unsanitized External Content in Agent Prompt **OWASP Agentic Security Index**: ASI-01 — Prompt Injection **Affected files**: - `python/packages/autogen-ext/src/autogen_ext/agents/web_surfer/_prompts.py` (lines 14, 33, 46) - `python/packages/autogen-ext/src/autogen_ext/agents/web_surfer/_multimodal_web_surfer.py` (line 885) ### Vulnerability Details The web surfer agent retrieves page metadata via Playwright and interpolates it directly into prompts sent to the LLM: **Prompt templates** (`_prompts.py:14`, `:33`): ```python # Line 14 (multimodal prompt) and line 33 (text prompt): - contents found elsewhere on the CURRENT WEBPAGE [{title}]({url}), in which case actions like scrolling... ``` **QA prompt** (`_prompts.py:46`): ```python def WEB_SURFER_QA_PROMPT(title: str, question: str | None = None) -> str: base_prompt = f"We are visiting the webpage '{title}'..." # <-- attacker-controlled ``` **Title source** (`_multimodal_web_surfer.py:883-885`): ```python title: str = self._page.url try: title = await self._page.title() # <-- controlled by website's <title> tag except Exception: pass ``` The `title` value comes from `page.title()`, which returns whatever the website sets in its `<title>` HTML tag. issue_title: Discussion: deterministic compiled subflows for predictable tool sequences
issue_body: ## Context Many agent workflows mix two different kinds of steps: 1. steps that genuinely require model reasoning; 2. predictable tool/data transformation steps that should run deterministically once the plan is known. LangGraph already provides a strong graph abstraction for controlling agent workflows. In practice, some parts of a graph may not need an LLM call at every step and may benefit from being treated as deterministic, replayable subflows. ## Problem When predictable tool sequences are handled as normal agent steps, teams can end up with: * unnecessary model calls; * harder replay/debugging; * more variance between runs; * less clear failure boundaries; * more expensive execution; * more complicated testing of deterministic logic. This is not a bug in LangGraph. It is more of a pattern question: how should users structure workflows where part of the process should be compiled or treated as deterministic once inputs are known? ## Proposal Would the LangGraph docs benefit from a pattern or guide for deterministic compiled subflows? The guide could cover when to separate: * model-routed graph steps; * deterministic tool chains; * replayable validation/enrichment steps; * parallel deterministic branches; * LLM interpretation steps after deterministic execution. Possible framing: ```text Plan/reason with the model where uncertainty exists. Run deterministic subflows where the execution path is known. Return structured results to the graph for interpretation or next-step routing. ``` ## Use cases * ETL-like tool chains inside agent workflows. * Deterministic validation

issue_title: Feature Request: Too strict dependency version pinning (`==`) causes dependency conflicts in complex projects
issue_body: ### What is the problem that your feature request solves? Description Currently, most Python dependencies in the project are pinned to exact versions using `==`, which makes it difficult to integrate `browser-use` into larger, more complex Python projects where other packages may require different versions of shared dependencies. Problem Exact version pins create unnecessary dependency resolution conflicts when: Using `browser-use` alongside other libraries that require newer or older versions of common dependencies (like `pydantic`, `requests`, `playwright`, etc.) Maintaining internal company projects with curated dependency sets where version ranges are preferred over exact pins Trying to upgrade individual dependencies to get security patches or bug fixes without waiting for a new `browser-use` release ### What is your proposed solution? Consider using more flexible version ranges using `>=` with upper bounds (like `>=2.0,<3.0`) instead of exact `==` pins for most dependencies, where possible. This would: Make the library much easier to integrate into existing projects Still protect against breaking changes from major version upgrades Allow users to get patch/minor updates for dependencies automatically Alternatively, you could keep exact pins for the published package but make the requirements.txt/pyproject.toml use looser constraints for development, or provide a separate variant with loose constraints. issue_title: Proposal: optional Agent Threat Rules security wrapper for autogen-ext
issue_body: AutoGen runs LLM-driven agent loops that often invoke shell, browser, file, and MCP tools. The same threat patterns that motivated work like the recent importlib provider hardening fix at #7463 also surface as content-level threats: prompt injection in tool outputs, exfiltration domains in agent-generated URLs, dangerous shell invocations passed to code executors, and credential leakage in messages. There is no first-class place in autogen-agentchat or autogen-ext today for content-level threat detection on the message or action boundary. I would like to propose adding an optional security scan extension under autogen-ext that wraps a BaseChatAgent and runs ATR-style detection on incoming messages or outgoing actions before they propagate. Reference for the rule set is the open Agent Threat Rules project at https://github.com/Agent-Threat-Rule/agent-threat-rules. ATR is Apache-2.0 and ships 330 rules across 9 categories, including prompt injection, exfiltration, dangerous shell commands, credential leakage, and tool-poisoning patterns. issue_title: Discussion: should AutoGen agents discover tasks from external open markets at runtime?
issue_body: **RFC-style discussion — not a feature request. Looking for design feedback.** ## Context AutoGen agents today receive their task from a human-initiated conversation or a predefined script. This works well for orchestrated workflows but creates a ceiling for fully autonomous operation: **an agent can't discover new work to do without human input**. ## Design question Has the AutoGen team considered a `TaskMarketAgent` or `Marketplace` abstraction where agents can autonomously poll external open task markets for available work? Rough idea: - An agent polls an external endpoint listing open tasks (with reward + requirements) - It accepts tasks matching its capabilities - It submits results back to the market - The market verifies and releases payment The agent loop becomes: discover → execute → submit → repeat. No human in the loop. ## Questions for the community 1. Is there an existing AutoGen pattern for agents that generate their own work queue from external sources? 2. issue_body: ## Problem In multi-agent AutoGen setups, agents that coordinate through message passing or tool calls have no way to express their capacity constraints as part of their definition. This creates a class of cascading failure that's hard to debug: Agent A retries when Agent B is saturated, each retry consumes Agent B capacity and generates more Agent A load, and the cascade amplifies until something times out or hits a hard resource limit. issue_title: Tool execution governance — delegation check before tool.forward()
issue_body: smolagents runs tool-calling agents with a minimal footprint. The agent picks tools and executes them. The trust model: if the tool is in the agent's toolbox, it can be called with any arguments. When agents run in production with tools that have side effects — writing files, calling APIs, sending messages — "the tool is available" isn't the same as "the agent is authorized to use this tool right now, for this task, with these arguments." Governance wraps tool execution: ```python from agent_passport_system import create_delegation, govern_action # Task-specific delegation delegation = create_delegation( delegated_to=agent_key, delegated_by=operator_key, scope=["tool:web_search", "tool:python_interpreter"], # no tool:file_write, no tool:email spend_limit=2000, expires_in_seconds=600 ) # Agent tries to use a tool outside scope → blocked before execution result = govern_action( action={"type": "tool:file_write", "path": "/etc/passwd", "content": "..."}, delegation=delegation, passport=agent_passport ) # Blocked. Signed receipt proves the boundary held. ``` The integration point is the tool execution path. Before `tool.forward()` fires, delegation is checked. Every call produces an Ed25519-signed receipt — permit or deny, with the full authorization context. Fits the smolagents philosophy: minimal, composable, one function to wrap tool execution. `pip install agent-passport-system` (v0.8.0, Apache-2.0) or `npm install agent-passport-system` (v1.36.2).

issue_title: Bug: CDP connection instability causing indefinite hangs with remote browsers
issue_body: ### Browser Use Version 0.12.5 ### Bug Description, Steps to Reproduce, Screenshots # Individual CDP calls within handlers lack timeouts, causing indefinite hangs with remote browsers ## Summary When using browser-use with remote browsers via CDP (e.g., Browserless), individual CDP calls like `Runtime.evaluate` inside `DOMWatchdog.on_BrowserStateRequestEvent` can hang indefinitely if the CDP WebSocket connection becomes stale. There is no per-call timeout — the only safety net is the event-level timeout (default 30s), which wastes the entire timeout window before failing. ## Environment - browser-use 0.12.5 - Remote browser via CDP (Browserless) - `keep_alive=True` ## Observed behaviour When running sequential agents on the same browser session with `keep_alive=True`, there are naturally idle periods between agent runs where no CDP traffic flows. After such an idle period, the next `BrowserStateRequestEvent` can hang: 1. `DownloadsWatchdog` completes but its CDP call (`get_current_page_url`) takes **3.0s** instead of the usual **0.00-0.01s** — an early signal the connection is degraded 2. `DOMWatchdog` enters `_get_pending_network_requests` 3. `get_or_create_cdp_session(focus=True)` succeeds but also takes **3.0s** 4. The subsequent `Runtime.evaluate` call **never returns** — no error, no timeout, just an indefinite await 5. The handler blocks until the event-level timeout fires The connection degradation is **not deterministic** — sometimes connections survive long idle periods, sometimes they become stale after relatively short gaps. No CDP errors or WebSocket close frame

issue_body: ## Summary `context_token_estimate` is set to `llm_adapter.usage.total_tokens` (input + output tokens) at line 1099 of `letta_agent_v3.py`. The post-step compaction check at line 1232 compares this inflated value against the context window. Because `total_tokens` includes output tokens (and reasoning/thinking tokens when applicable), the check triggers compaction even when the actual in-context message content is well under the threshold. issue_title: [Feature Request] Memory Poisoning Protection for AutoGen Agents via OWASP Agent Memory Guard
issue_body: ## Problem AutoGen agents with persistent memory and teachability are vulnerable to **memory poisoning attacks** — adversarial inputs stored in agent memory can cause agents to leak secrets, ignore instructions, or produce corrupted outputs in future conversations. OWASP identifies this as a top risk for LLM applications. ## Proposed Solution **OWASP Agent Memory Guard (AMG)** is an open-source Python library that wraps any memory store as a transparent security layer: - `pip install agent-memory-guard` - Scans every memory write for prompt injection, PII leakage, and tampering - 92.5% detection rate on AgentThreatBench benchmark - Works with any memory backend (vector stores, conversation history, teachability DB) ## Links - GitHub: https://github.com/OWASP/www-project-agent-memory-guard - PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/agent-memory-guard/ - Benchmark: https://pypi.org/project/agent-threat-bench/ Would the AutoGen team consider integrating AMG as a security layer for agent memory? Happy to contribute a PR.

issue_title: Proposal: Agent Identity Verification for GroupChat Participants
issue_body: ## Summary AutoGen's GroupChat enables multiple agents to collaborate in open conversation. However, there is no mechanism to verify the identity of participating agents. Any agent can send messages with no authentication of identity. ## Problem - GroupChat accepts agents with no identity verification - No way to distinguish a trusted internal agent from an unverified external one - In cross-organizational scenarios, this creates attack surface: agent spoofing, unauthorized participation, prompt injection from untrusted sources ## Proposal Add an optional `identity_provider` parameter to GroupChat that validates each agent's credentials before allowing participation: ```python group_chat = GroupChat( agents=[agent_a, agent_b, agent_c], identity_provider=AgentIDProvider(policy="require_verified"), ) ``` Each agent presents a cryptographic credential on join. The identity provider verifies it and allows or denies participation. Fully opt-in and backward-compatible. ## Reference Implementation [AgentID](https://getagentid.dev) provides: - ECDSA P-256 certificates per agent - Verification API for real-time credential validation - Trust scores based on provenance and behavior - Agent registry for discovery and audit We have built integrations for CrewAI, LangChain, and MCP. Repository: [github.com/haroldmalikfrimpong-ops/getagentid](https://github.com/haroldmalikfrimpong-ops/getagentid) Happy to contribute an AutoGen integration.

issue_title: Governance/audit checks for browser automation agents in CI
issue_body: Browser automation agents are one of the higher-risk agent patterns since they interact with live web content and user data. In production, teams will need to demonstrate audit trails, kill switches, and policy enforcement around these actions. Right now there's nothing in CI that validates whether agent files have these governance patterns in place. A PR-level check could catch gaps early - missing error handling around browser actions, no logging, no human approval for sensitive operations. I built a GitHub Action ([asqav-compliance](https://github.com/jagmarques/asqav-compliance)) that does this kind of scan for agent frameworks including browser-use. But curious if there's interest in native support or a recommended approach for governance validation in the project.

issue_title: RFC: Efficient Bi-directional Event Loading for V1 Conversations
issue_body: ## Problem V1 conversations with long event histories experience slow load times because: 1. **WebSocket replays ALL historical events one-by-one** (no batching, no compression) 2. **REST prefetch and WebSocket duplicate work** - both fetch the same events 3. **Users wait to see the current state** while oldest events load first For a 500-event conversation, this means 500 individual WebSocket messages and potential double-fetching of the entire history. ## Proposed Solution: Bi-directional Event Loading Load events from both ends of the timeline simultaneously: ``` Timeline: [oldest] ←←←← REST (backwards) ←←←← [newest] →→→→ WebSocket (forward) →→→→ [new events] ``` ### Flow 1. **REST fetches newest events first** (`sort_order=TIMESTAMP_DESC`) 2. **User sees current state immediately** 3. **WebSocket connects with** `after_timestamp` parameter (set to oldest REST event timestamp) 4. **WebSocket only delivers NEW events** after that timestamp - zero duplication 5. **REST continues paginating backwards** in background, prepending older events ### Benefits * **Instant perceived load**: User sees most recent/relevant state immediately * **Zero duplication**: REST handles history, WebSocket handles future * **Efficient transfer**: REST batching + compression for bulk data * **Real-time from start**: WebSocket connected early for live updates ## Implementation Status <!-- linear:table-colwidths:266,266,266 --> | Component | Status | Details | | -- | -- | -- | | `after_timestamp` WebSocket param (agent-server) | ✅ Done | [software-agent-sdk#1880](<https://github.com/OpenHands/soft

issue_body: The SDK already ships `on_tool_start` / `on_tool_end` and a set of guardrail examples — `input_guardrails.py`, `output_guardrails.py`, `llm_as_a_judge.py`. One pattern that falls between these is an **external governance gate**: a second opinion that isn't the same model, running before high-stakes tool execution, with a signed verifiable proof attached. `llm_as_a_judge.py` uses the model to grade its own output. issue_title: OpenAIProvider ignores API-reported context_length, defaults all unknown models to 30k tokens
issue_body: ## Problem When using OpenAI-compatible providers (e.g. Synthetic.new) that correctly report `context_length` in their `/v1/models` response, Letta stores `max_context_window: 30000` in the `provider_models` table instead of the actual value. This happens on every server restart, reverting any manual DB fixes. ## Root Cause `OpenAIProvider._do_model_checks_for_name_and_context_size` (and its async variant) accept a `length_key` parameter defaulting to `"context_length"` — but never actually read it from the model dict. They unconditionally call `get_model_context_window_size[_async]()`, which looks the model up in litellm specs. For models not in those specs (anything custom or not yet indexed), the lookup falls through to `LLM_MAX_CONTEXT_WINDOW["DEFAULT"]` = **30000**. **The chain:** 1. Synthetic.new `/v1/models` returns `context_length: 262144` for `hf:moonshotai/Kimi-K2.5` 2. `OpenAIProvider` ignores the response field entirely 3. Litellm spec lookup finds nothing for this model 4. Falls back to `DEFAULT` = 30000 5. 30000 is stored in `provider_models` DB 6. Repeats on every restart This affects **any** model served through a generic `OpenAIProvider` that isn't in litellm's bundled spec list. ## Proposed Fix Both the sync and async methods should check the API response first, falling back to litellm/defaults only when the API doesn't provide a value: ```python if length_key in model and model[length_key]: context_window_size = model[length_key] else: context_window_size = await self.get_model_context_window_size_async(model_name) ``` This matches the pattern already use

issue_title: Feature request: delete_protected flag to prevent agent self-deletion
issue_body: ## Problem Letta Code agents with Bash access can trivially delete themselves by calling `curl -X DELETE` against the agents API endpoint or using the SDK. This has been reported as happening in production twice -- across Letta Code 0.18.x and 0.21.x, with servers 0.16.4 and 0.16.7. The agent simply decides during normal work to delete itself, and nothing stops it. **Client-side mitigations exist** (PreToolUse hooks with exit code 2, `permissions.deny` patterns in `.letta/settings.json`), but these can be circumvented by obfuscation (base64 encoding, writing to a script file then executing, etc.) and don't protect against SDK-based deletion paths. ## Proposed Solution Add a `delete_protected` boolean flag on agents that the `DELETE /v1/agents/{agent_id}` endpoint checks before proceeding. Behavior: - When `delete_protected = true`, the DELETE endpoint returns a 403 or 409 with a clear error message - The flag is settable/unsettable via `PATCH /v1/agents/{agent_id}` (so the owner can still remove protection when needed) - Default: `false` (no breaking change) Yes, an agent could theoretically PATCH the flag off and then DELETE itself -- but that requires two deliberate steps with specific intent, which is a much higher bar than a single `curl -X DELETE`. The goal isn't perfect tamper-proofing; it's raising the barrier enough that an agent won't accidentally self-destruct during normal work. ## Why Not Just Client-Side Hooks? issue_title: Pandas serialization/deserialization logic with msgpack
issue_body: Right now, users can use pandas series/dataframes in state and serialize them with a `JsonPlusSerializer` that has `pickle_fallback` enabled. It'd be great to have these as first class citizens, able to be serialized via `msgpack` like `numpy` arrays. This is a bit of a tricky task, as dataframes have lots of nuanced features like: * multiindexes (both row and column) * dtypes by column * opportunity for arbitrary objects in table cells We want to preserve df structure during serialization and deserialization. There are a few options here, assuming we continue to use msgpack: * Dump pickled content (this is a bit redundant, both are serialization protocols). One benefit here is that pandas x pickle work well together with all of the above nuances * Dump bytes directly, though custom logic will have to be written for the above pandas features * Use `arrow` - this is the most efficient storage wise, though there are some type inconsistencies (like with `object` dtype) that will need to be considered. A PR addressing this should have thorough testing, perhaps mimicking many of the conditions tested for in https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/pull/5057. You might want to reference https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/pull/5035 as a reference for how to add logic for new types to `JsonPlusSerializer`.

issue_title: fix: log level warning → error for HTTP 4xx/5xx responses in automation service event forwarding
issue_body: ## Why `_send_source_to_automation_service` has three failure paths. PR #14820 raised the log level from `warning` to `error` for transport-level failures (`asyncio.TimeoutError`, `aiohttp.ClientError`), but the HTTP response failure path was left at `warning`: \`\`\`python # enterprise/server/services/automation_event_service.py if resp.status >= 400: ... logger.warning( # <-- should be logger.error f'[AutomationEventService] Automation service returned ' f'{resp.status} for {source} org {org_id}: {body}' ) \`\`\` A `>= 400` response (including 408 Request Timeout, 504 Gateway Timeout, 5xx errors) means the event was not delivered — same user impact as a transport failure. Logging it as `warning` is inconsistent with the convention established in #14820: - `warning` = degraded but recoverable (retrying, falling back) - `error` = operation failed, user impact, no recovery ## What to change Change `logger.warning` to `logger.error` at the `resp.status >= 400` branch in `_send_source_to_automation_service`, and add a corresponding test to verify the level. ## Related Surfaced during review of #14820.

issue_title: Customizing traces and spans: Ability to add metadata to spans
issue_body: It would be great if we could customize span_data for any given span. The metadata field only works for the top level trace, but child spans like `response_span` do not have any existing metadata (nor the ability to add such metadata) such as current_turn, agent_name etc that is useful for querying data. I think a simple solution for now could be to use the AgentHooks to manipulate the current_span and add any metadata you like. ``` def on_llm_start(..., agent: str, ...): current_span = get_current_span() # response span current_span.span_data["custom_metadata"] = agent.name ``` To do this, all spans would need to start before the _start hooks are called and finish after the _end hooks are called. This is not standardized currently. Agent span follows this pattern, while response span starts after the `on_llm_start` hook and ends before the `on_llm_end` hook, making it difficult to manipulate the span data.

issue_body: ### Component Core / Python SDK ### Description ### Summary `AsyncMemory.reset()` hardcodes `delete_col()` unconditionally, bypassing the `VectorStoreFactory.reset()` optimisation that `Memory.reset()` already uses. Sync `Memory.reset()` checks `hasattr(self.vector_store, "reset")` and calls `VectorStoreFactory.reset()` when available — which resets the store in-place without tearing it down and recreating it. issue_title: [Feature Request]: Add sqlite-vec Vector Store Integration
issue_body: ### Feature Description Add support for sqlite-vec as a vector store backend in LlamaIndex. [sqlite-vec](https://github.com/asg017/sqlite-vec) is a lightweight, zero-dependency SQLite extension for vector similarity search written in pure C. It supports float, int8, and binary vector types, and runs anywhere SQLite runs — including Python, Node.js, and edge environments. The proposed integration would implement a `SqliteVecVectorStore` class extending `BasePydanticVectorStore`, supporting: - Vector storage and cosine/L2 similarity search via SQLite virtual tables - Metadata filtering on stored documents - Persistent and in-memory modes (just like SQLite itself) - Standard LlamaIndex operations: `add()`, `query()`, `delete()`, `get_nodes()`, `clear()` ### Reason LlamaIndex doesn’t currently support a SQLite-based vector store integration. While there are embedded options like DuckDB and FAISS, SQLite is the most widely used database engine globally and is already a part of many Python projects. For users looking for a simple, local-first RAG pipeline without relying on external services, the options are limited: 1. They can run a separate vector database (like Chroma, Qdrant, or Milvus). 2. They can use DuckDB, which might not fit into their existing setup. 3. They can opt for FAISS, but it doesn’t offer built-in persistence or metadata filtering. This is why we welcome sqlite-vec — it requires no server or extra infrastructure and uses a database format that developers are already familiar with. ### Value of Feature - **No setup needed**: Just use a local .db file — perfect

issue_body: ### Description `Topic.from_checkpoint` and `NamedBarrierValue.from_checkpoint` assign the checkpoint's container directly to the new channel instead of copying it: ```python # topic.py empty.values = checkpoint # named_barrier_value.py empty.seen = checkpoint ``` `BaseChannel.from_checkpoint` documents that "If the checkpoint contains complex data structures, they should be copied", and the channels' own `copy()` methods do copy (`self.values.copy()`, `self.seen.copy()`), but `from_checkpoint` does not. So two channels restored from the same checkpoint object share the same list/set, and an in-place update to one mutates the checkpoint and the sibling. ### Reproduction ```python from langgraph.channels.topic import Topic source = Topic(str, accumulate=True) source.update(["a", "b"]) checkpoint = source.checkpoint() one = Topic(str, accumulate=True).from_checkpoint(checkpoint) two = Topic(str, accumulate=True).from_checkpoint(checkpoint) one.update(["c"]) print(two.get()) # ['a', 'b', 'c'] -> expected ['a', 'b'] print(checkpoint) # ['a', 'b', 'c'] -> checkpoint was mutated ``` `NamedBarrierValue` (and `NamedBarrierValueAfterFinish`) behave the same way with their `seen` set. issue_body: ## Browser Use Version 0.13.1 (latest) ## Environment - Windows 11, headless (no desktop GUI) - Python 3.12.10, WindowsProactorEventLoopPolicy (default) - Chromium 145.0.7632.6 (Playwright-installed) - cdp-use: 1.4.5, websockets: 15.0.1, httpx: 0.28.1 ## Summary After systematic investigation, I identified **three layered root causes** that together make browser-use CDP layer unstable on Windows — while Playwright direct `launch()` works perfectly in the same environment. This is not a single bug but an architectural mismatch. Related to existing issues: #1830, #3533, #2613, #4579, #4688. --- ## Root Cause 1: httpx.ReadError — CDP HTTP startup race + proxy leakage **Location**: `BrowserSession.connect()` → `httpx.AsyncClient().get("/json/version")` **Evidence**: 1. If `HTTP_PROXY` is set (common on Windows with Clash/V2Ray), aiohttp routes 127.0.0.1 through the proxy → 502. 4. Even without proxy, there is a **race window** on Windows: Chromium startup has a ~1-2s gap between TCP port open (aiohttp poll succeeds) and HTTP server fully initialized (httpx request can fail with `ReadError`). issue_title: bug: tool exceptions are caught and replaced with generic error messages — lose root cause
issue_body: ## Problem When a tool raises an exception during execution, CrewAI catches it and replaces the full traceback with a generic error string like `"Error: tool execution failed"`. The original exception type, message, and traceback are discarded. Create a custom tool that raises `ValueError("invalid parameter: count must be positive")` 2. Configure a crew to use this tool 3. The agent receives only "Error: tool execution failed" with no indication of what went wrong ## Expected Behavior The full exception should be available to: 1. The agent (so it can adapt its strategy — retry, fix input, skip tool) 2. The user/logs (for debugging) 3. At minimum, a structured error object with `type`, `message`, and `traceback` fields ## Proposed Fix ```python # Instead of: return f"Error: tool execution failed" # Return: return json.dumps({ "error": True, "type": type(e).__name__, "message": str(e), "retryable": isinstance(e, (TimeoutError, ConnectionError)), }) ``` ## Related - #5930 (PDF tool errors are swallowed) - #5990 (Deepseek format errors are opaque)

issue_title: UnicodeDecodeError on Windows: open() without encoding='utf-8' in validation.py crashes on GBK locale
issue_body: ## Description `langgraph_api/validation.py:13` reads `openapi.json` without specifying encoding: ```python with open(pathlib.Path(__file__).parent.parent / "openapi.json") as f: openapi_str = f.read() ``` On Windows with Chinese (GBK) or Japanese (CP932) locale, Python's `open()` defaults to the system encoding instead of UTF-8. This crashes with: ``` UnicodeDecodeError: 'gbk' codec can't decode byte 0x94 in position 1660: illegal multibyte sequence ``` The byte `0x94` comes from the UTF-8 encoding of an em dash (`—`, U+2014) in `openapi.json`: ``` "...not documented here — OpenAPI 3.1 does not describe WebSocket..." ``` The UTF-8 sequence `\xe2\x80\x94` is valid UTF-8 but illegal in GBK. ## Reproduce On Windows with Chinese system locale: ```powershell .venv\Scripts\python.exe -m langgraph_cli dev --config langgraph.json ``` ## Affected versions - 0.10.0 - 0.12.0.dev2 (latest dev) 0.8.7 worked because `openapi.json` didn't contain em dash at that time. ## Fix ```python with open(pathlib.Path(__file__).parent.parent / "openapi.json", encoding="utf-8") as f: ``` ## Workaround ```powershell $env:PYTHONUTF8=1 ``` ## Related Same root cause fixed in: - langchain-ai/langchain#17995 - Aider-AI/aider#3853 - unslothai/unsloth#2660

issue_title: Feature: Cryptographic action receipts (AAR) for multi-agent conversation provenance
issue_body: ## Cryptographic Action Receipts for Multi-Agent Conversations In AutoGen's multi-agent conversation patterns, agents pass messages, invoke tools, and make decisions — but there's no standardized way to prove what happened. For enterprise deployments requiring audit trails, this is a gap. ## Agent Action Receipts (AAR) AAR is an open standard for Ed25519-signed proof of agent actions. Each action produces a tamper-proof receipt: - **Agent identity + action + scope** - **SHA-256 hashes** of inputs/outputs (PII-safe by design) - **Ed25519 signature** — offline-verifiable, no network calls needed Receipts chain via **Session Continuity Certificates (SCC)** — a hash chain proving an agent maintained consistent identity across conversation turns. ## AutoGen integration concept An `AARMiddleware` agent wrapper that signs receipts on every `generate_reply`: ```python from autogen import AssistantAgent from botindex_aar import AARMiddleware agent = AARMiddleware( AssistantAgent("analyst", llm_config=llm_config), signing_key=key ) # Every reply now carries a .receipt attribute ``` ## What's available - Spec (IETF-style): https://github.com/Cyberweasel777/agent-action-receipt-spec - npm SDK: https://www.npmjs.com/package/botindex-aar (115+ daily downloads) - Hosted signing: $0.001/receipt, SCC anchoring: $0.01/anchor - Landing: https://aar.botindex.dev Already in discussion at crewAI (#4754), FINOS AI Governance (#266), and AWS Agent Squad (#429). Feedback welcome on how this maps to AutoGen's middleware patterns.

issue_title: Feature: Cryptographic receipts for agent tool execution (AAR)
issue_body: ## Problem smolagents executes tools on behalf of users — code execution, web search, API calls. Each tool run produces a result but no cryptographic proof that the tool actually ran with those specific inputs and produced that specific output. For multi-agent systems, enterprise deployments, and agent commerce, verifiable action provenance is becoming a requirement. ## Proposal Integrate [Agent Action Receipts (AAR)](https://github.com/Cyberweasel777/agent-action-receipt-spec) into the tool execution pipeline: ```python # Conceptual: receipt-aware tool execution class VerifiableTool(Tool): def forward(self, *args, **kwargs): result = super().forward(*args, **kwargs) receipt = create_receipt( agent_id=self.agent.name, action={'tool': self.name, 'args_hash': sha256(str(args))}, output_hash=sha256(str(result)), ) return result, receipt ``` Each agent run produces a receipt chain — verifiable by any party with the agent's public key. ### What AAR provides - Ed25519 signatures over canonicalized JSON per action - SHA-256 input/output hashing (verifiable without exposing raw data) - Receipt chaining across multi-step tool use - Compatible with [Mastercard Verifiable Intent](https://www.mastercard.com/us/en/news-and-trends/stories/2026/verifiable-intent.html) and [x402 (Coinbase)](https://github.com/coinbase/x402) ### SDK TypeScript: `npm install botindex-aar` (live, MIT) Python: in development - Spec: https://github.com/Cyberweasel777/agent-action-receipt-spec - Landing: https://aar.botindex.dev

issue_title: Agent with checkpointer=True: forking human message produces duplicate human messages in new branch
issue_body: ## Summary When a parent graph invokes an agent built with `checkpointer=True` (`create_agent(..., checkpointer=True)` or `create_deep_agent(..., checkpointer=True)`), forking a human message via a past `checkpoint_id` produces a branch that contains **both the original human message and the forked one**, instead of only the new one. ## Repro Parent graph invokes an agent with `checkpointer=True`. No interrupts. 1. User sends "hi" → agent replies. State: `[human("hi"), ai(...)]`. 2. Fork with `checkpoint_id=<pre-human>` and new input `human("hi2")`. Expected new branch state: `[human("hi2"), ai(new)]`. **Actual**: `[human("hi"), human("hi2"), ai(new)]` — old human message carried over into the new branch. Reproduces with both `create_agent` (langchain) and `create_deep_agent` (deepagents). ## Affected versions - Confirmed on langgraph **1.1.9**. - Appears pre-existing — not a regression from a specific PR, looks like a long-standing interaction between parent fork logic and the agent's internal checkpointer. ## Workaround - Setting `checkpointer=False` avoids this duplication on 1.1.6, but on 1.1.7+ hits the separate #7592 regression, leaving no fully working configuration on recent versions. ## Env - Python 3.13 - langgraph 1.1.9 - deepagents 0.5.3 / langchain (latest)

issue_title: feat: MCP tool error isolation — individual tool failures should not abort entire agent run
issue_body: ## Problem When an AutoGen agent uses MCP tools (via `mcp-tools` integration) and a single tool fails, the error propagates up and aborts the entire agent run. This is problematic because: 1. **One bad tool kills the session**: If the agent calls 5 tools and the 3rd fails (e.g., MCP server timeout, tool-specific error), the remaining 2 tool calls are lost 2. **No per-tool error reporting**: The agent receives a generic "MCP tool call failed" error, not structured error information about which tool failed and why 3. **No retry/fallback**: There's no mechanism for the agent to retry the failed tool or use an alternative In production multi-agent scenarios, individual tool failures should be surfaced as tool-level errors that the agent can reason about and recover from, not as fatal exceptions. ## Expected Behavior 1. MCP tool errors should be caught and returned as structured `ToolResult` with `is_error=True` rather than raising exceptions 2. The agent should see: "Tool `search_docs` failed: Connection timeout (MCP server at localhost:9000)" 3. The agent run should continue with remaining tool calls 4. Optional: configurable retry policy per tool/MCP server ## Current Workaround Users must wrap every MCP tool call in try/except in their agent logic, which defeats the purpose of declarative tool registration. ## Related - AutoGen's MCP tool integration: `autogen-ext[mcp]` - MCP Python SDK transport error handling: modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk#1764

issue_title: Orphaned tool messages after mid-run crash block all future runs
issue_body: ## Description When a run crashes mid-tool-sequence (timeout, rate limit, context overflow, etc.), `tool_call` and `tool_return` messages can end up split across different runs. The orphaned side (typically `tool_return` without a matching `tool_call`, or vice versa) persists in the agent's `message_ids`. On the next run, the LLM provider rejects the entire request because tool call/result pairing is strictly enforced. This permanently blocks the agent -- every subsequent message attempt fails with the same pairing error until the orphaned messages are manually removed. ## Error (OpenAI) ``` INVALID_ARGUMENT: Bad request to OpenAI-compatible endpoint: Error code: 400 - {'error': {'message': 'No tool call found for function call output with call_id call_XXXXX.', 'type': 'invalid_request_error', 'param': 'input', 'code': None}} ``` Anthropic equivalent would be `unexpected tool_use_id found in tool_result blocks`. ## Root Cause Letta's run boundary handling does not clean up unpaired tool messages when a run fails mid-tool-sequence. The tool_call is persisted in one run's context, and the tool_return (or approval_request/approval_response) ends up in a subsequent run or orphaned entirely. Once stored in `message_ids`, the broken pairing blocks all future runs. ## Observed Data In one affected agent (GPT-5.4 with reasoning): - 20 out of 37 messages in `message_ids` were broken - 7 orphaned `tool_return_message` entries with no matching `tool_call` - 7 `approval_request`/`approval_response` pairs whose associated tool_returns were the orphans - Same agent hit this twice in 48 h

issue_title: [Feature] Runtime behavioral trust scoring for tool calls via MCP Observatory
issue_body: ## Problem When agents call external tools (MCP servers, APIs, third-party services), there's no runtime mechanism to evaluate whether that tool is behaving normally *right now*. Static allow-lists don't catch a previously-trusted server that starts returning malformed data, timing out intermittently, or exhibiting anomalous latency patterns. The Agents SDK currently trusts all configured tools equally. ## Proposal Add an optional **behavioral trust scoring hook** that runs before each tool invocation, using runtime telemetry from the [Dominion Observatory](https://dominion-observatory.sgdata.workers.dev) — a behavioral trust registry tracking 14,800+ MCP servers with anonymized latency, success rate, and anomaly data. The hook would: 1. **Before tool call**: query the Observatory for the tool server's current trust score (cached with configurable TTL) 2. **Policy decision**: based on a configurable threshold, either proceed, warn, or block the call 3. **After tool call**: report anonymized telemetry (server_url, success, latency_ms — no prompts, no tool arguments, no user data) back to the Observatory ## What this looks like ```python from agents import Agent, Runner from dominion_observatory import check_trust, report # As a guardrail / hook async def trust_gate(ctx, tool_call): result = check_trust(tool_call.server_url) if result.trust_score and result.trust_score < 40: raise ToolBlockedError( f"Trust score {result.trust_score} below threshold for {tool_call.server_url}" ) agent = Agent( name="my-agent", tools=[...], before_tool_call=trust_gate, # proposed hook point ) `

issue_title: Add Tensorlake sandbox provider for persistent agent-scoped tool execution
issue_body: **Motivation** E2B sandboxes are ephemeral — each tool call gets a fresh sandbox and the previous state is destroyed. This works for stateless tools, but agents that accumulate state across multiple tool calls (installing packages, writing intermediate files, building up an environment) pay the full cold-start cost on every invocation. **Proposal** Add [Tensorlake](https://www.tensorlake.ai/sandboxes) as a sandbox provider. Tensorlake sandboxes are persistent and agent-scoped: each agent gets a named sandbox that Tensorlake suspends when idle and resumes on the next call. Files and installed packages carry over across tool invocations without re-creation. **Key behaviors**: - Agent-scoped named sandboxes (letta-agent-<id>) with suspend/resume lifecycle - Environment fingerprinting to detect config changes and recreate sandboxes when needed - Name-based rediscovery after server restart with fingerprint validation - Snapshot support (TENSORLAKE_SNAPSHOT_ID) to skip cold-start package installs - Auto-detection: setting TENSORLAKE_API_KEY + installing letta[tensorlake] is all that's needed **Limitations for now**: - TypeScript tools not supported (falls back to E2B/Modal) - agent_state round-trip requires a pre-built snapshot with letta installed - Per-agent or per-tool sandbox type selection not supported (same as E2B/Modal) I have an implementation ready for this on a fork, happy to open a PR if I can get contributor access. You can find the branch at https://github.com/tensorlakeai/letta/tree/sw/add-tensorlake-sandbox

issue_title: ENH: Add pre-tool-call authorization layer to MultiStepAgent
issue_body: smolagents has excellent sandboxing (E2B, Modal, Docker, local Python) — but `MultiStepAgent.step()` dispatches tool calls with no authorization layer. Sandboxing prevents system compromise, but doesn't answer: "was this agent authorized to call this tool?" The Open Agent Protocol (OAP) defines a `before_tool_call` standard (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.18901596) that fits naturally into smolagents' tool dispatch: a `GuardrailProvider` protocol checked before every tool call, with a built-in `AllowlistProvider` for simple cases and the protocol open for custom implementations. Would you be open to a PR that adds a `guardrail` parameter to `MultiStepAgent` — a `GuardrailProvider` evaluated in `step()` before `tool(**args)` executes? Denied calls would return a structured error observation rather than raising, so the agent can adapt without crashing. Reference implementation https://github.com/bytedance/deer-flow/pull/1240

issue_title: Race condition in get_or_create_claude_code_agent creates duplicate agent pairs on startup
issue_body: **Describe the bug** When Claude Code CLI sends parallel requests on initial startup (e.g., topic detection + main request), `get_or_create_claude_code_agent` creates duplicate primary + sleeptime agent pairs due to a check-then-act race condition. **Root cause**: The function at `letta/server/rest_api/proxy_helpers.py:458-571` has no concurrency control: ```python # Line 501-506: Check if agent exists agents = await server.agent_manager.list_agents_async(...) # Line 510-521: If found, return if agents and len(agents) > 0: return agent # Line 561-566: If not found, create new_agent = await server.create_agent_async(...) ``` When two requests arrive simultaneously, both see "no agent exists" and both create one. **Evidence from database**: ```sql SELECT id, name, created_at FROM agents ORDER BY created_at; ``` | id | name | created_at | |----|------|------------| | agent-584915d3... | claude-code-user-000 | 07:36:37.326633 | | agent-67da3117... | claude-code-user-000 | 07:36:37.326636 | | agent-57298aa3... | claude-code-user-000-sleeptime | 07:36:37.504233 | | agent-439a7fe9... | claude-code-user-000-sleeptime | 07:36:37.505529 | The 3 microsecond gap between primary agents confirms parallel creation. **Impact**: - Orphaned agents remain in database - Potential for both sleeptime agents to run (we observed 29 runs vs 1 run) - Wasted resources on initial startup **Suggested fix options**: 1. Add database unique constraint on agent name (reject second insert) 2. Use application-level locking (asyncio.Lock per user) 3. Upsert pattern (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING + SELECT)

issue_title: Azure embedding requests return 404 - malformed URL construction
issue_body: **Description** When using Azure as the embedding provider for folders/sources, file uploads fail during the embedding phase with a 404 Resource Not Found error. The root cause is a malformed URL being constructed with a duplicate /embeddings path segment. The embedding_endpoint stored in EmbeddingConfig is pre-constructed with the full path including /embeddings?api-version=.... However, when the OpenAI Python SDK's client.embeddings.create() method is called, it automatically appends /embeddings to the base URL. This results in the path appearing twice: **Expected URL** `POST https://<azure-resource>.cognitiveservices.azure.com/openai/deployments/text-embedding-3-small/embeddings?api-version=2024-02-15-preview` **Actual URL** `POST https://<azure-resource>.cognitiveservices.azure.com/openai/deployments/text-embedding-3-small/embeddings?api-version=2024-02-15-preview/embeddings` **Steps to reproduce** 1. Configure Letta with Azure embedding provider 2. Create an agent with Azure embeddings 3. Create a folder using the agent's embedding configuration 4. Upload a file to the folder 5. Observe 404 errors in the logs during the embedding phase **Suggested Fix** The embedding_endpoint should either not include the /embeddings suffix (letting the SDK add it), or be used as the complete URL without the SDK appending additional path segments. The fix is likely in letta/llm_api/azure_client.py or wherever the Azure embedding endpoint URL is constructed. **Setup** Letta self-hosted 0.16.2

issue_title: Trailing-slash redirects use HTTP scheme behind HTTPS proxies, breaking Authorization forwarding
issue_body: ## Bug Description When Letta is deployed behind an HTTPS-terminating reverse proxy (Cloudflare Tunnels, nginx, Traefik, etc.), API endpoints that trigger trailing-slash redirects generate `Location: http://...` URLs instead of `Location: https://...`. This causes HTTP clients that follow redirects (including Node.js `fetch()`) to strip the `Authorization` header per the [Fetch specification](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#http-redirect-fetch), resulting in `401 Unauthorized` errors. ## Root Cause In [`letta/server/rest_api/app.py`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/main/letta/server/rest_api/app.py), `uvicorn.run()` is called without `proxy_headers=True`, so Starlette doesn't respect `X-Forwarded-Proto` when generating redirect URLs. There is even a commented-out middleware for this: ```python # Add reverse proxy middleware to handle X-Forwarded-* headers # app.add_middleware(ReverseProxyMiddleware, base_path=settings.server_base_path) ``` ## Reproduction **Setup:** Letta v0.16.4 behind Cloudflare Tunnel (TLS terminated at edge, forwarded as HTTP to Letta) ```bash # This triggers a 307 redirect with http:// Location header $ curl -v -X POST "https://letta.example.com/v1/conversations?agent_id=agent-xxx" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $LETTA_API_KEY" # Response: # < HTTP/2 307 # < location: http://letta.example.com/v1/conversations/?agent_id=agent-xxx # ^^^^ # Should be https:// # Adding trailing slash manually bypasses the redirect and works: $ curl -X POST "https://letta.example.com/v1/conversations/?agent_id=agent-xxx" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $LETTA_API_KEY" # => 2

issue_title: Feature request: semantic search over memfs files
issue_body: ## Summary Memfs (context repositories) is positioned as the successor to both memory blocks and archival memory. However, it currently only supports exact-match search (grep, glob) with no semantic/embedding-based search capability. Since archival memory -- which memfs is partially replacing -- had semantic search as a core feature, this creates a regression for users who rely on conceptual/fuzzy retrieval over their agent's long-term knowledge. ## Use case An agent with dozens of memfs files covering different topics needs to find relevant information without knowing the exact file or keyword. Today the agent must either: 1. Maintain a manual index file (table of contents) describing each file's contents 2. Grep with broad patterns and read through results hoping for relevance 3. Already know which file to look for None of these scale well as the memory corpus grows. ## Proposed behavior Add an optional embedding index over memfs files so agents can perform semantic search across their memory filesystem. For example, if a user first says "My favorite football player is Ronaldo" and later says "My current favorite football player is Messi", the current flow can store both facts as separate ADD memories. issue_title: InMemoryStore keeps stale vectors after index=False updates
issue_body: ﻿## Description `InMemoryStore` leaves stale vectors behind when an existing key is updated with `index=False`. A minimal sequence is: ```python from langgraph.store.memory import InMemoryStore store = InMemoryStore(index={"dims": dims, "embed": embeddings}) store.put(("test",), "doc1", {"text": "zany zebra Xerxes"}) store.put(("test",), "doc1", {"text": "new text about dogs"}, index=False) results = store.search(("test",), query="Zany Xerxes") ``` The second `put(..., index=False)` updates the stored value, but the old vector for `doc1` remains in `_vectors`, so `doc1` can still be returned with a similarity score for the old text. ## Expected behavior Updating an existing key with `index=False` should clear previously stored embeddings for that key. The item may still appear as a scoreless result depending on search pagination behavior, but it should not retain a stale score from the previous value. ## Local patch prepared I have a small branch prepared here: https://github.com/onyx679/langgraph/tree/codex/clear-memory-store-vectors-on-index-false Commit: `cc2e544` The patch clears existing vectors for updated keys before inserting any new vectors, and adds sync/async regression tests. ## Validation ```text # Red before implementation: python -m pytest tests\test_store.py::test_vector_update_with_index_false_clears_existing_embedding tests\test_store.py::test_async_vector_update_with_index_false_clears_existing_embedding -q # 2 failed, both retained the old similarity score # After implementation: python -m pytest tests\test_store.py::test_vector_update_with_index_false_c

issue_title: create_react_agent silently terminates on Gemini MALFORMED_FUNCTION_CALL instead of retrying or raising
issue_body: ## Issue When using `create_react_agent` with Google Gemini (gemini-2.5-flash), the agent silently terminates without making any tool calls when the LLM returns `finish_reason: MALFORMED_FUNCTION_CALL`. The `should_continue` node sees no tool calls and routes to END, giving the user no indication that the LLM failed to generate valid JSON. ## Expected Behavior The agent should either: 1. **Retry** the LLM call (ideally with exponential backoff) 2. **Raise an exception** so the application can handle it 3. At minimum, **log a warning** that the LLM returned a malformed function call ## Current Behavior The agent silently terminates with 0 tool calls. The only way to detect this is by inspecting `response_metadata.finish_reason` in LangSmith traces or manually checking the last message. ## Reproduction ```python from langgraph.prebuilt import create_react_agent from langchain_google_genai import ChatGoogleGenerativeAI from langchain_core.tools import tool @tool def search(query: str) -> str: """Search the knowledge base.""" return f"Results for: {query}" llm = ChatGoogleGenerativeAI(model="gemini-2.5-flash", temperature=0.0) agent = create_react_agent(model=llm, tools=[search]) # This query intermittently triggers MALFORMED_FUNCTION_CALL with Gemini for event in agent.stream({"messages": [("user", "what is RTO")]}): pass # Check the last message last_msg = event["messages"][-1] print(last_msg.response_metadata.get("finish_reason")) # Outputs: "MALFORMED_FUNCTION_CALL" (no tool calls made, agent terminated) ``` ## Environment - langgraph: 0.2.x - langchain-google-genai: latest

issue_body: ### Browser-Use Version 0.12.6 (latest main) ### Bug Description `SecurityWatchdog._is_url_allowed()` unconditionally allows `data:` and `blob:` scheme URLs **before** checking `allowed_domains` / `prohibited_domains`: ```python # security_watchdog.py L181-183 if parsed.scheme in ['data', 'blob']: return True ``` This means when a user configures `allowed_domains=['example.com']` to restrict navigation, the agent can still navigate to arbitrary content via `data:` URLs. The agent itself warns users about this at `agent/service.py:533`: ``` ⚠️ Agent(sensitive_data=••••••••) was provided but Browser(allowed_domains=[...]) is not locked down! ⚠️ ☠️ If the agent visits a malicious website and encounters a prompt-injection attack, your sensitive_data may be exposed! ``` Users who follow this guidance and set `allowed_domains` believe they are protected. issue_title: Use shallow clone by default with a setting to fetch full Git history
issue_body: ## Problem Starting conversations from large repositories can be slow because OpenHands currently performs a full Git clone when a repository is selected. For most tasks, OpenHands only needs the current branch and recent repository state. Fetching the full Git history by default adds unnecessary startup time, especially for very large repositories. Some tasks still require full Git history — for example, tasks involving older commits, tags, merge bases, historical blame, changelog generation, or checking out arbitrary commits. Users should have a clear way to opt into the previous full-clone behavior when they need it. ## Proposed solution Make shallow cloning the default for repository selections. Add a setting under **Application → Git Settings** or a new **Repository Cloning** section: **Fetch full Git history for repositories** Default: **Off** When this setting is off, OpenHands uses a shallow clone to speed up repository startup. When this setting is on, OpenHands uses the previous full-clone behavior. Suggested helper text: > OpenHands uses shallow clones by default to speed up startup for large repositories. Turn this on if your tasks require full Git history, tags, merge bases, historical blame, or checking out older commits. Full clones may take longer for large repositories. ## User experience Users should not need to understand Git clone flags to get faster repository startup by default. issue_title: TypeScript SDK silently drops plain-string / reasoning-model memory items (Python parity gap)
issue_body: Parity follow-up surfaced during review of #5880. In `mem0-ts/src/oss/src/memory/index.ts`, when a reasoning model emits `{"memory": ["User likes coffee"]}`, the strict `AdditiveExtractionSchema` (`z.object({ text: z.string() })`) Zod parse throws, the catch block assigns the raw array directly, and `extractedMemories.map((m) => m.text ?? "").filter(t => t.length > 0)` silently discards all plain-string items — no crash, no warning, memory lost. The Python fix in #5880 (`normalize_extracted_memories`) does not carry over. A TS `normalizeExtractedMemories` mirroring the Python normalizer (plain string, `{text}`, `{fact}`, single-key key-as-fact) would close the gap. Related: #5901 (Python side, fixed in #5880).

issue_title: LLM extraction transport failures silently swallowed (returned [] instead of raising)
issue_body: Tracking issue for the bug fixed in #5878 (salvage of #5178). `_add_to_vector_store` (sync `main.py:914-916`, async `2538-2540`) caught all exceptions from `llm.generate_response` and returned `[]`, making LLM transport failures (rate limits, connection errors) indistinguishable from "LLM succeeded but extracted nothing". Callers had no way to detect or retry. **Fix (#5878):** re-raise transport failures wrapped in `LLMError(...) from e` on both paths, while the *parse* failure at `main.py:929-931` still returns `[]` (an LLM that responded with empty/invalid JSON did succeed). Async regression test added. Follow-up: TS SDK has the identical `catch (e) { return []; }` pattern at `index.ts:855-858`. Fixed by #5878.

In letta/functions/async_composio_toolset.py, the execute_action() method initiates an asynchronous external API call using aiohttp.ClientSession() without specifying a timeout parameter. By default, aiohttp applies a 300-second (5-minute) global timeout when none is provided. When the Letta Agent interacts with real-world 3rd-party SaaS via Composio, unreliable network conditions or API tarpit delays will force the session.post operation to hang for up to 5 minutes per request. In a highly concurrent task bus, this lack of fail-fast configuration will quickly drain and starve all available worker coroutines, effectively stalling the entire Agent's event loop and rendering it unresponsive. What did you expect to happen? A defensive, explicit system-level or framework-level timeout (e.g., aiohttp.ClientTimeout(total=15)) should be injected into the session instantiation. This ensures a "fail-fast" behavior, throwing a timeout exception promptly to free up the event loop instead of silently starving the task scheduling bus. ### How are you running Letta? issue_title: bug: no automatic page-crash recovery — agent hangs after browser tab crashes
issue_body: ## Bug Description When a browser page crashes (e.g., due to memory exhaustion from heavy JavaScript, WebGL context loss, or renderer process crash), the agent has no automatic recovery mechanism. The agent hangs indefinitely waiting for page state that will never come. ## Steps to Reproduce 1. Configure browser-use agent to navigate a heavy SPA (e.g., complex React app with large state) 2. Allow the agent to interact with the page over multiple steps 3. When the page's renderer crashes (indicated by Playwright/Chromium page crash event), the agent: - Cannot detect that the page is dead - Continues trying to find elements that don't exist - Never reloads or restores state ## Expected Behavior The agent should: 1. Detect page crash events (via Playwright `page.on('crash')` or similar) 2. Automatically reload the page and attempt to restore navigation state 3. If recovery fails, report the crash as a tool error rather than hanging ## Actual Behavior Agent retries element selectors in a loop, eventually exhausting its step budget with "element not found" errors. The root cause (page crash) is never logged or surfaced. ## Relevant Code The page lifecycle is managed via Playwright, which emits crash events. The agent's step loop does not appear to register a crash handler or check page health between actions. ## Impact - Agent tasks fail silently with confusing timeout errors - No way for users to distinguish between page crash vs legitimate element-not-found - Wasted API credits as agent retries against a dead page

issue_title: BUG: Object Lifecycle Hijacking via Unrestricted Dunder Methods in Custom Class Definitions within LocalPythonExecutor
issue_body: Problem LocalPythonExecutor maintains a persistent state dictionary to preserve variable context across consecutive execution steps. However, when evaluating custom class definitions in evaluate_class_def, the interpreter does not validate or restrict method names. This allows the executed code to arbitrarily define sensitive magic/dunder methods (e.g., __del__, __eq__, __getattribute__). Once these objects with malicious dunder methods are instantiated and left in the state dictionary, they act as "time bombs". When the host environment (e.g., the evaluation pipeline) later triggers garbage collection (GC) or performs state comparisons on these variables, the host Python interpreter automatically invokes these dunder methods. This enables malicious logic to escape the sandbox's execution window (completely bypassing timeout decorators and MAX_OPERATIONS limits) and execute covertly on the host's main timeline, leading to state manipulation, resource leaks, or host process crashes. Steps to reproduce This is a structural flaw in the AST evaluation logic. issue_title: [Feature Request] Memory checkpoint validation to prevent poisoning attacks
issue_body: ## Problem LangGraph agents with persistent memory (via checkpointers like MemorySaver, SqliteSaver, PostgresSaver) are vulnerable to memory poisoning. Adversarial content stored in checkpoints persists across invocations and can influence agent behavior indefinitely. ## Proposed Solution Add optional memory validation via [OWASP Agent Memory Guard](https://github.com/OWASP/www-project-agent-memory-guard) at checkpoint write time: ```python from agent_memory_guard import scan_memory from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver class SecureMemorySaver(MemorySaver): def put(self, config, checkpoint, metadata, new_versions): # Validate memory content before persisting for channel, value in checkpoint['channel_values'].items(): if isinstance(value, str): result = scan_memory(value) if result.blocked: raise MemoryPoisoningError(result.reason) return super().put(config, checkpoint, metadata, new_versions) ``` ## Context - OWASP Incubator project, 5,400+ downloads - Already integrates with LangChain - arXiv:2606.04329 (June 2026) proves memory poisoning bypasses standard defenses - Adopted by UK AI Safety Institute

The manager has no way to distinguish between "task completed with empty output" and "task failed". Reason: max_steps (2) reached without calling final_answer. ``` This gives the manager enough signal to either retry with a different approach, escalate, or report failure cleanly. ## Notes - This applies to both `CodeAgent` and `ToolCallingAgent` as sub-agents - The fix is in `ManagedAgent.__call__` - cat

issue_title: Add Weaviate Engram long-term memory layer for chat and agent apps
issue_body: ### Summary Dify has no long-term/external memory layer; conversation memory is only `TokenBufferMemory` (a read-only window over the `Message` table). This proposes an **opt-in, default-off** integration with [Weaviate Engram](https://docs.weaviate.io/engram), the managed memory service. ### Motivation Engram turns raw conversation turns into durable, scoped memories and serves them via hybrid retrieval, letting apps improve over time without growing every prompt. It's a natural fit for Dify's chat/agent apps. ### Proposed change (config-gated, default-off) - New `ENGRAM_ENABLED` / `ENGRAM_API_KEY` / `ENGRAM_ENDPOINT` / `ENGRAM_RECALL_TOP_K` settings. - `core/memory/engram`: a thin wrapper over the `weaviate-engram` SDK with `store()` / `recall()`. SDK imported lazily; all calls best-effort (errors logged, never raised) so memory I/O cannot break generation. - **Store**: a `message_was_created` signal handler writes the completed user/assistant turn fire-and-forget (covers chat + agent-chat). - **Recall**: the chat runner searches relevant memories and folds them into the prompt context alongside dataset retrieval. Note: Engram is a managed Weaviate Cloud service, so this is a cloud client integration (API key), not a docker-compose addition. ### Scope New `core/memory/engram` module + config + a signal handler + chat-runner recall. `weaviate-engram` added as a dependency group. Unit-tested with a mocked client. I'd like to work on this and have a PR ready.

issue_title: Optional Weaviate native multi-tenancy, vector compression, and advanced index options
issue_body: ### Summary The Weaviate vector backend currently uses one collection per dataset with no multi-tenancy, no vector compression, and no configurable index/distance settings. This proposes adding these as **opt-in, default-off** options. ### Motivation - At scale, one-collection-per-dataset creates thousands of collections. Weaviate native multi-tenancy (one shared collection, many isolated tenants) is the intended pattern for this. - Vector compression (RQ/PQ/BQ/SQ) and index-type selection (hnsw/flat/dynamic) reduce memory/storage cost and are currently unavailable. ### Proposed change (all default-off, backward compatible) - `WEAVIATE_MULTI_TENANCY_ENABLED`: new datasets sharing an embedding model become tenants in one shared collection (tenant = dataset id). Existing datasets keep their persisted layout (recorded in `index_struct`). - `WEAVIATE_COMPRESSION` (rq/pq/bq/sq) + tuning knobs; flat index restricted to bq. - `WEAVIATE_INDEX_TYPE` (hnsw/flat/dynamic) + `WEAVIATE_DYNAMIC_INDEX_THRESHOLD` + `WEAVIATE_DISTANCE_METRIC`. Dynamic index requires `ASYNC_INDEXING=true` on the server (added to compose). - Optional `WEAVIATE_REPLICATION_FACTOR`. ### Scope All changes confined to `api/providers/vdb/vdb-weaviate/` + config + compose env. Existing behavior is unchanged when flags are off. Depends on the 1.38/client-4.22 upgrade (#38211). I'd like to work on this and have a PR ready.

issue_title: Silent exception swallowing in Property Graph LLM Path Extractors
issue_body: ### Description Currently, `DynamicLLMPathExtractor`, `SchemaLLMPathExtractor`, and `SimpleLLMPathExtractor` all catch `Exception` / `ValueError` broadly during extraction and return an empty triplet list `[]` while logging an error message. This swallowed exception behavior makes it impossible for downstream code (like asynchronous orchestrators, bulk ingestion pipelines, or UI layers) to gracefully catch, halt, or bubble up critical failures such as LLM API timeouts or output validation constraints. The silent failure hides the true source of the problem, leading to "empty graph" results that are extremely difficult to debug. ### Expected Behavior There should be an option to propagate these exceptions upward instead of silencing them, allowing the caller to decide how to handle the failure (e.g. abort the pipeline, retry, etc.). *(I have a local repro and a complete fix for this pattern across the property graph module, and will link a PR shortly.)*

issue_body: Hey Smolagents team, Been using Smolagents for a multi-tool code generation pipeline and ran into something that's been causing me real headaches in production. When the HuggingFace Inference API is overloaded (which happens more than you'd think during peak hours), `HfApiModel` just... hangs. No timeout, no error, no recovery. When the API is slow or overloaded, it waits forever. 2. **No retry logic** — As the docs mention, `run()` doesn't catch exceptions internally. The official stance is that users should build their own retry wrapper: ```python # From the docs — users are expected to write this themselves def run_agent_with_retry(agent, query, max_retries=3): for attempt in range(max_retries): try: return agent.run(query) except Exception as e: if 'overloaded' in str(e).lower() or '429' in str(e): time.sleep(2 ** attempt) e

issue_body: ### Checked other resources - [x] This is a bug, not a usage question. - [x] I searched existing issues and didn't find a duplicate (related but distinct: #8217 covers the `awrap_tool_call` wrapper path). - [x] I reproduced on the latest `main`. ### Description When a tool calls `interrupt()` (directly, or via human-in-the-loop tooling), the resulting `GraphInterrupt` is reported on the `tools` stream channel as a **`tool-error`** event, with `message=str(error)`. issue_title: Agent governance: deterministic permission gating for browser actions
issue_body: ## Context browser-use agents control a real browser — they navigate, click, fill forms, and extract data. Currently, any agent with browser access can perform any browser action. There's no mechanism to say "the product scraper agent may GET pages but not POST forms" or "the QA agent may click buttons but not navigate to non-whitelisted domains." The recent agchk audit (#4739) flagged this: `capability_policy` at HIGH and the observation that "Permission policy is not enforced on all dispatch paths." ## The problem Without deterministic permission gating, browser-use agents inherit the full browser surface. This creates risks: 1. **Domain escalation**: An agent tasked with scraping `example.com/docs` navigates to `example.com/admin` 2. **Action escalation**: An agent allowed to read page content instead submits forms or triggers downloads 3. **Data exfiltration**: An agent fills forms with sensitive data and submits to external endpoints 4. **Indirect prompt injection**: An agent navigates to a page with hidden instructions that redirect its behavior ## Proposal: Deterministic browser action gating Add an optional policy layer that evaluates before every browser action: ```python # Browser policy at agent creation agent = Agent( task="Scrape product pages", browser_policy={ "allowed_domains": ["example.com/products/*"], "allowed_actions": ["navigate", "extract_content", "screenshot"], "require_approval_for": ["click", "fill_form", "submit"], "denied_actions": ["download", "execute_js"] } ) ``` At action time, the framework checks: 1. Is this domain allowed? → deterministic

issue_title: perf(memory): N+1 MessageFile queries in TokenBufferMemory.get_history_prompt_messages
issue_body: ### Summary `TokenBufferMemory.get_history_prompt_messages` loads message files with **two `MessageFile` queries per message** (one for user files, one for assistant files), i.e. **2N+1** database round-trips for an N-message history (N capped at 500). This method runs on every chat / agent-chat / advanced-chat turn that uses conversation memory, so long conversations cause a large number of DB round-trips on a hot path. ### Where `api/core/memory/token_buffer_memory.py` → `get_history_prompt_messages`: ```python for message in messages: user_files = db.session.scalars( select(MessageFile).where( MessageFile.message_id == message.id, (MessageFile.belongs_to == "user") | (MessageFile.belongs_to.is_(None)), ) ).all() ... assistant_files = db.session.scalars( select(MessageFile).where( MessageFile.message_id == message.id, MessageFile.belongs_to == "assistant" ) ).all() ``` ### Proposal Batch-load the files with two `IN` queries keyed by `message_id` (constant 3 queries total: 1 messages + 2 files), grouping in Python. Filter semantics stay identical (user files still include `belongs_to IS NULL`); the returned prompt messages are unchanged. This is in the spirit of prior perf work (e.g. #29483, #33014). I have a small patch ready (~+64/-9, including a regression test that asserts a constant query count) and will open a PR linking this issue. ### Environment - Affected: 1.14.x and current `main`
